extracted.intended_audience: advanced students and researchers in classical mechanics / mathematical physics (historical Newtonian-style treatment)
extracted.subtask_description: Derivations and constructive procedures to determine trajectories, velocities, times, and related geometric areas for bodies acted on by given centripetal force laws (including inverse-square and other power laws), with special constructions for conic-section orbits and nearly circular orbits (apsidal motion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXII — Spaces described under inverse-square centripetal force
rubrics_metrics.description: Posito quod vis centripeta sit reciproce proportionalis quadrato distantiæ locorum a centro, spatia definire quæ corpus recta cadendo datis temporibus describit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives a constructive method: associate the conic section (ellipse, hyperbola, parabola) whose umbilicus and axis relate to the fall-line; areas (e.g., ASD, ABD, BDEB) are proportional to time. Handles three cases (ellipse, hyperbola, parabola) and prescribes limiting procedures (reduce latus rectum to zero) to recover rectilinear descent. Includes geometric constructions (semicircles, perpendiculars) to find the distance fallen in given time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXIII (Theor. IX) — Relation between falling velocity and circular velocity
rubrics_metrics.description: With previously found constructions, the velocity of a falling body at a point C is to the velocity of a body describing a circle about center B at distance BC in the ratio which is half that of CA to the figure's principal semidiameter ½AB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishes proportional relations via limiting arguments on conic sections and uses relationships among conic elements (CP, SY, AO, AC, etc.). Provides a geometric limit process: as the conic's latus rectum decreases to zero, various lines converge and yield the velocity ratio AC:AO (i.e., explicit geometric dependence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXIV (Theor. X) — Parabolic special case for velocity
rubrics_metrics.description: If the figure BED is a parabola, the falling body's velocity at any point C equals the velocity with which a body could uniformly describe a circle with radius equal to half the interval BC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived by letting the parabola's latus rectum shrink and using previous corollaries; provides a simpler concrete relation for the parabola (half-radius correspondence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXV (Theor. XI) — Equal-area correspondence to uniform circular motion
rubrics_metrics.description: The area of the figure DES described by radius SD (with SD indefinite) equals the area which a body, describing a circle of radius equal to half the latus rectum of DES about center S uniformly, could describe in the same time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives two cases (circle/hyperbola and parabola). Proves equality by comparing infinitesimal generated area elements KSk and SDd, using limiting arguments and relations between velocities of falling and circular motions; yields a method to equate times with areas via corresponding circular motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXVI (Prob. XXV) — Determining descent times from a given place
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct the space fallen in a given time for a body falling from a given initial distance from the center, using semicircle constructions (semicircle ADS and equal semicircle OKH about S) and equality of areas ASD and section OSK.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical geometric construction: erect ordinates, join SD, equate areas, and use Theorem XI equivalence to deduce the distance descended in the given time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXVII (Prob. XXVI) — Times of ascent/descent for a projected body
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a body projected up or down from a given place with any velocity, determine the times of ascent or descent by comparing the square of that velocity to the uniform circular velocity and constructing a circle of radius CA equal to half AS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescribes taking CA proportional to half AS in the ratio of the square of the given velocity to the uniform circular velocity; identifies whether the case yields a parabola, circle, or hyperbola depending on that ratio (2:1 boundary). Then uses previous theorems (Theorem X, IX, XI) and sector/area equalities to find times and positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXVIII (Theor. XII) — Sine and versed-sine proportionalities under linear central force
rubrics_metrics.description: If the centripetal force is proportional to the altitude (distance from the center), then the times, velocities, and spaces described by falling bodies are proportional respectively to arcs of sines, sines of arcs (i.e., versed sines), and squares of sines/versed sines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives corollaries: equal times correspond to equal quadrant arcs and hence all bodies falling from any given distances take equal times to reach the center. Established by analogy to Proposition XI and earlier methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXIX (Prob. XXVII) — From any centripetal law and quadratures find velocities and times
rubrics_metrics.description: Given any law of centripetal force and given curve quadratures, determine a falling body's velocities at each place and the times to reach any place; and conversely, given velocities or times, determine the central force law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides the prescription: the velocity at a location E is proportional to the side of the square (i.e., square root) of a certain curvilinear area ABGE; time to describe a segment equals a corresponding curvilinear area ALME. The proof uses infinitesimal partitioning, nascent ratios, and the connection between increments of velocity and generated areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XL (Theor. XIII) — Equal-altitude velocity equality across different motions
rubrics_metrics.description: If two bodies, one moving under any central force in any curve and another moving rectilinearly (or otherwise), have equal velocities at some equal altitude, then their velocities at all equal altitudes are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows via constructing concentric circles and resolving forces into transverse and normal components; by comparing accelerations generated in equal times one finds velocities at corresponding altitudes remain equal. Corollaries: applies to pendula and perfectly lubricated impediments, and furnishes general formulae for velocity as root of differences of powers when force ∝ A^{n-1}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XLI (Prob. XXVIII) — Constructing trajectories and times from centripetal law
rubrics_metrics.description: Given any centripetal force law and given quadratures, determine the trajectory in which the body will move and the times at which it will be at given points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: construct auxiliary circles and secants, form small neighboring points I and K, introduce a height A such that a falling body would acquire at D the same velocity as at I, define a quantity Z = Q/A representing IK/KN, relate ABFD and Z to find quantities YX×XC etc., and then construct the trajectory curves whose infinitesimal elements correspond to these rectangles. The method yields the locus for the body after a given elapsed time and allows finding apsides and angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XLII (Prob. XXIX) — Motion from given position and velocity along a given straight line
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a central force law and an initial point and velocity directed along a given straight line, determine the ensuing motion of the body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct by equating a given uniform centripetal rectilinear reference (PDRQ) to the actual law, use previous Problem XXVIII constructions to obtain curves (ALMm, BFGg, abzv, dcxw) and, from the given rectangle and angle CIT, determine the quantity Q and hence the trajectory and the body's altitude after any given time (area equalities give locus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XLIII (Prob. XXX) — Making a body move in a given trajectory while another remains at rest
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that a body can be made to move in any given curve about a center of forces while another body remains at rest in the same trajectory, by suitably choosing an angular motion (rotation) of the frame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: revolve the given orbit in the plane with an angular relation between VCp and VCP so that area described by constructed Cp corresponds proportionally to time; choose the centripetal force of appropriate magnitude to produce the same instantaneous motion in the rotating configuration. Uses the Corollary to Proposition VI and shows how to find the centripetal force required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XLIV (Theor. XIV) — Difference of forces for moving vs. stationary orbits
rubrics_metrics.description: The difference between the forces that move a body equally in a fixed orbit and in the same orbit rotating (revolving) is in the triple (cubic) ratio of the common altitude inverse (i.e., proportional to 1/A^3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derives by comparing corresponding infinitesimal transverse and central motions in the fixed and moving orbits; gives corollaries with explicit formulae for elliptical orbits (expressing the additional force needed for the moving orbit in terms of ellipse parameters, latus rectum, semidiameters, and values G and F related to angular ratios). Provides universal expressions (X + {(RG^2 - RF^2)}/A^3) for the centripetal force in general altitude A and recipes to adjust angular speed to obtain new immobile orbits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XLV (Prob. XXXI) — Apsidal motion for nearly circular orbits
rubrics_metrics.description: For orbits that are very nearly circular, determine the motion of the apsides (precession) by arithmetic expansion: let T be maximum altitude, A a general altitude, X = T - A and expand the centripetal law in powers of X to extract the terms producing apsidal motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: express the centripetal force (e.g., uniform case) as a series in (T - X) and collate numerator terms; take limiting nearly-circular case (R≈T, X→0) to simplify to leading-order terms; deduce rate and character of apsidal advance. Provides an example for uniform centripetal force producing a leading-order proportionality G^2 : T^2 etc.
